title: An Introduction to Bordeaux: Left Bank & Right Bank, Classic & New Wave

sources.note: Availability researched live across six Mexican online wine retailers. Per-store raw findings are saved as <store>_list.json in this same folder.

stores_browsed.bordeaux_depth: very deep (221 SKUs, all five First Growths plus Pétrus, Cheval Blanc, Ausone, garagiste cuvées)
moderate, no dedicated Bordeaux collection so results were gathered via site search (~60 relevant SKUs found)
small but focused around André Lurton and Château Angelus (~24 SKUs)

introduction:
Bordeaux is the axis around which the entire fine-wine world still turns. Tucked into the Atlantic-facing southwest of France around the Gironde estuary and its two feeder rivers, the Garonne and the Dordogne, it is less a single wine region than a federation of terroirs, châteaux, and rival philosophies that has been shipping wine to the world since the Romans planted vines here and the medieval English, who ruled Aquitaine for three centuries, developed an enduring thirst for 'claret.' To love Bordeaux is to love blends: almost nothing here is bottled as a single grape. Instead, each estate composes its wine every vintage from a small palette of varieties, balancing power, perfume, and structure the way a chef balances a sauce.

The single most useful idea for a newcomer is the split between the Left Bank and the Right Bank of the Gironde. On the Left Bank — the Médoc and Graves/Pessac-Léognan, running north from the city of Bordeaux along the estuary's western shore — the soil is famously poor and gravelly, deposited over millennia by the Garonne and the Pyrenees. Gravel drains fast, forces vine roots deep in search of water, and radiates heat back onto the fruit at night. This is Cabernet Sauvignon country: a thick-skinned, late-ripening grape that thrives in this warmth-banking soil and rewards patience, giving wines built on firm tannin, cassis and graphite fruit, cedar and tobacco-leaf aromatics, and a capacity to age for decades. It was the Left Bank's grandest châteaux that were ranked in the 1855 Classification, commissioned by Napoleon III for the Paris World's Fair, which sorted the Médoc's best estates (plus one Graves outlier, Haut-Brion) into five tiers of Cru Classé — a hierarchy so entrenched that, in 170 years, only one wine has ever been promoted (Mouton Rothschild, from second to first growth, in 1973).

Cross the water to the Right Bank — Saint-Émilion, Pomerol, and their satellite appellations — and the terroir flips: cooler clay and limestone, sometimes iron-rich clay called 'crasse de fer', that holds moisture and suits Merlot's earlier-ripening, softer-tannined nature, often rounded out with Cabernet Franc. Right Bank wines tend to be plusher and more perfumed in youth — red plum, black cherry, mocha, violets — though the best age just as gracefully as their Left Bank cousins. Saint-Émilion has its own classification, revised roughly every decade (most recently and controversially in 2022), crowned by a small handful of Premiers Grands Crus Classés 'A'. Pomerol, home to Pétrus and Le Pin, has never been classified at all — a point of pride for a district that built its reputation purely on what is in the glass.

A newcomer should also know that Bordeaux is not only red. The gravelly communes of Pessac-Léognan and Graves make some of the world's great dry whites from Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, textured and age-worthy in a way most Sauvignon Blanc never is. And along the Garonne's Sauternais bend, morning river mist and afternoon sun create the perfect breeding ground for Botrytis cinerea — 'noble rot' — which shrivels Sémillon grapes into raisin-like concentration, yielding the honeyed, saffron-and-apricot dessert wines of Sauternes and Barsac, Château d'Yquem chief among them.

Finally, Bordeaux is not a museum. Since the early 1990s a genuine 'new wave' has reshaped how the region is made and sold. On the Right Bank, a handful of self-taught outsiders — most famously Jean-Luc Thunevin, working out of an actual garage in Saint-Émilion — proved that a tiny, meticulously farmed plot could out-perform grand historic estates, birthing the so-called 'garagiste' movement and forcing the classification system to eventually recognize wines like Valandraud that the old guard had first dismissed. Elsewhere, ambitious families like the Cathiards at Smith Haut Lafitte or Hubert de Boüard at Angelus poured modern agronomy, gravity-flow cellars, and relentless attention to detail into estates that then muscled their way up the official rankings on merit. And grand names like Haut-Brion and Mouton Rothschild now also bottle more accessible 'everyday luxury' labels — Clarendelle, Le Petit Mouton — built to bring first-growth expertise to tables that will never see a first-growth price tag. The selections below are built to let you taste both halves of that story: the classical, gravel-and-limestone establishment that built Bordeaux's reputation, and the restless new wave that keeps proving it still has more to say.

wines.why_this_wine: This is the ideal front door into Left Bank Bordeaux: real Haut-Médoc gravel terroir and a real Cabernet-led blend, at a price that lets you drink it on a Tuesday rather than save it for an anniversary. It shows the Left Bank grammar — structure, savory fruit, a herbal edge — without asking a novice palate to decode decades of bottle age.
wines.tasting_notes: Deep ruby color. Blackcurrant, plum, and a touch of cedar and graphite on the nose, with a savory, tobacco-leaf undertone typical of Cabernet-driven Haut-Médoc. On the palate it is medium-to-full bodied with firm, structured tannins, moderate acidity, and a finish that leans toward dried herbs and dark fruit rather than sweetness — built for a grilled ribeye or lamb.
wines.winery_info: Château Beaumont sits in Cussac-Fort-Médoc, between the more famous communes of Margaux and Saint-Julien, on a substantial 75-hectare gravel-mound vineyard. It is part of the Grands Millésimes de France portfolio (a joint venture historically tied to Crédit Agricole and Suntory), which has invested steadily in the property since the 1980s to make it one of the most reliable, widely-planted Cru Bourgeois names on export markets.
wines.historical_significance: Cru Bourgeois is the Médoc's 'second tier' classification, created in the 1930s and reformed several times since (most recently in 2020) specifically to recognize excellent Médoc châteaux that fall outside the fixed, unchangeable 1855 Grand Cru list. Beaumont is one of its steadiest performers, illustrating why the Cru Bourgeois tier exists: excellent, gravel-terroir Bordeaux does not require a Grand Cru label or a Grand Cru price.

wines.wine_name: Château Gruaud Larose, Saint-Julien, 2ème Grand Cru Classé
wines.grape_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
wines.why_this_wine: Gruaud Larose is the classic mid-priced case study in why Saint-Julien is considered the most 'complete' of the Médoc communes — it splits the difference between the perfume of Margaux and the power of Pauillac. As a Second Growth from a strong, ripe vintage, it over-delivers relative to price and shows what serious, age-worthy Left Bank structure tastes like before you commit First-Growth money.
wines.tasting_notes: Dense purple-ruby. Black cherry, blackcurrant liqueur, and cedar box aromas, layered with graphite, dried violets, and a whisper of clove from careful oak aging. The palate is full-bodied and powerfully structured, with ripe, grippy tannins and a long, savory finish — a wine that rewards a decanter tonight and rewards a cellar even more.
wines.winery_info: One of the largest and oldest estates in Saint-Julien, Gruaud Larose traces its vineyard to the 1720s under Abbot Gruaud, who reputedly flew flags over the property to signal harvest quality to sailors on the Gironde. It has been owned since 1997 by the Merlaut family through the Taillan group, which has invested heavily in the cellars while keeping the powerful, traditional house style intact.
wines.historical_significance: The estate's old motto, 'the wine of kings, the king of wines,' reflects its historic prestige as a Second Growth of the 1855 Classification — the tier just below the five First Growths, and often the tier connoisseurs consider the sweet spot of quality-to-price in the Médoc hierarchy.

wines.wine_name: Château Léoville Las Cases, Saint-Julien, 2ème Grand Cru Classé
wines.why_this_wine: This is the textbook 'Super Second' — a Second Growth on paper that critics and collectors routinely taste blind against, and sometimes above, the First Growths. The 2019 is a landmark vintage for the estate, and it is the single wine on this list most likely to make a serious collector's jaw drop.
wines.tasting_notes: Inky, dense purple. An intensely layered nose of cassis, blackberry, cedar, pencil shavings, and crushed stone, with underlying violet and dark chocolate notes. The palate is monumental: extremely fine, chalky tannins, remarkable freshness for its density, and a finish that unfurls for minutes. Built to be cellared for 20-30+ years.
wines.winery_info: Léoville Las Cases occupies the walled 'Grand Clos,' the single vineyard plot directly adjoining Château Latour — geography that tells you everything about its pedigree. It is run by the Delon family, whose exacting, almost obsessive selection (only the best barrels ever make the grand vin) has made this the most sought-after non-First-Growth in Bordeaux for over a generation.
wines.historical_significance: The original Léoville estate was, before the French Revolution, the single largest vineyard in the Médoc; it was split in the 19th century into Léoville-Las-Cases, Léoville-Poyferré, and Léoville-Barton, three separate 1855-classified châteaux that still bear the family name today. Las Cases retained the historic core, including the prized Grand Clos.

reviews.note: 2019 widely reviewed in the high-90s to 100-point range on release, cited among the vintage's most complete Saint-Juliens.

wines.wine_name: Château Mouton Rothschild, Pauillac, 1er Grand Cru Classé
wines.grape_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon (majority), Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
wines.why_this_wine: No wine better dramatizes Bordeaux's rigid, near-unchangeable class system — and its one great exception. Mouton is the only château ever promoted within the 1855 Classification, and the 2022 vintage, which landed a rare double-100-point score, is both a scientific and artistic peak: proof that Pauillac's gravel plateau can still produce perfection.
wines.tasting_notes: Opaque garnet-purple. A famously exotic, almost perfumed nose for Pauillac — cassis and black cherry laced with graphite, cedar, incense, and a signature note of fresh mint and spice box. The palate is opulent yet precise, with velvety, high-density tannins, remarkable freshness, and a finish that lingers for well over a minute.
wines.winery_info: Mouton Rothschild has been shaped since the 1920s by Baron Philippe de Rothschild, an aesthete and marketing visionary who pioneered château-bottling, and, from 1945, commissioned a different world-renowned artist (Braque, Dalí, Warhol, Bacon, and many more) to design the label every single vintage. The estate is now run by his daughter, Baroness Philippine, and her children.
wines.historical_significance: In the original 1855 Classification, Mouton was ranked only a Second Growth, a slight the Baron spent nearly 50 years contesting. In 1973, French Agriculture Minister Jacques Chirac finally approved its promotion to First Growth — the sole amendment in the Classification's history — inspiring Mouton's own defiant new motto: 'First, I am. Second, I was. Mouton does not change.'

wines.why_this_wine: Clarendelle is Bordeaux's modern answer to the question 'what if First Growth expertise came in an everyday bottle?' It represents the new-wave democratizing instinct of the last 30 years: grand houses building accessible, technically flawless labels rather than leaving the mid-market to lesser producers.
wines.tasting_notes: Bright ruby. Red and black currant fruit with soft floral lift and a touch of vanilla oak. Round, supple tannins and moderate acidity make it approachable and food-friendly right on release — no decade of cellaring required.
wines.winery_info: Clarendelle was created in 1996 by Prince Robert of Luxembourg, president of Domaine Clarence Dillon — the family company that owns Château Haut-Brion, Bordeaux's only Left Bank First Growth located outside the Médoc. Clarendelle is made and partly aged using Haut-Brion's own technical team and cellars, sourcing fruit from selected partner estates across the region.
wines.historical_significance: The label's name honors Clarence Dillon, the American banker who bought Haut-Brion in 1935. Clarendelle embodies a distinctly modern Bordeaux strategy: rather than dilute a legendary grand vin, a grand house builds a second, accessible brand engineered from the ground up to carry its winemaking philosophy to a much wider audience.

wines.wine_name: Le Petit Haut Lafite (second wine of Château Smith Haut Lafitte)
wines.classification: Second wine of a Cru Classé de Graves
wines.grape_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
wines.why_this_wine: This is the accessible expression of one of Bordeaux's most genuinely 'new wave' transformations: an estate remade from the ground up by hands-on owners obsessed with precision farming. It lets you taste the Cathiard family's philosophy — energy, purity, meticulous selection — for a fraction of the grand vin's price.
wines.tasting_notes: Medium-deep ruby. Fresh blackberry and red plum with cedar, a touch of graphite, and subtle toasted-oak spice. Silky, well-integrated tannins and lively acidity give it an energetic, precise character rather than sheer weight.
wines.winery_info: Smith Haut Lafitte was transformed after Florence and Daniel Cathiard, former Olympic ski racers turned entrepreneurs, purchased the estate in 1990. They rebuilt the vineyard practically from scratch, plow parts of it with horses, built their own on-site cooperage to control barrel quality, and lean on biodynamic-inspired viticulture and an in-house research lab.
wines.historical_significance: The Cathiards also founded Les Sources de Caudalie, the pioneering 'vinothérapie' spa built on the property that uses polyphenols from grape seeds and vine sap in its treatments — an almost unheard-of diversification that turned a wine estate into a global hospitality brand while never loosening its grip on viticultural detail.

wines.wine_name: Château Smith Haut Lafitte, Cru Classé de Graves
wines.grape_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
wines.why_this_wine: The grand vin in a legendary vintage: 2010 is considered one of the two or three greatest Bordeaux vintages of the 21st century, combining a hot, dry growing season with cool nights that preserved freshness. Tasting this alongside a classic Left Bank First Growth shows how far a determined, modernized non-classified-in-1855 estate has come.
wines.tasting_notes: Deep, dense garnet. Ripe black and red fruit — blackcurrant, black cherry — intertwined with graphite, cedar, and a distinct smoky, mineral edge from the gravel terroir. Powerful, densely-packed tannins framed by 2010's signature vibrant acidity, with a very long, mineral-driven finish that will reward 15-20+ years in the cellar.
wines.winery_info: See Le Petit Haut Lafite above — same estate, same Cathiard-family philosophy of precision farming and constant technical investment, expressed here at full intensity in the top selection of fruit from the property's best gravel parcels.
wines.historical_significance: Though outside the 1855 Médoc Classification, Smith Haut Lafitte was named a Cru Classé de Graves in 1959 for both its red and white wines — a rare dual distinction — and the Cathiard era since 1990 has pushed it into the conversation with the region's elite estates, a case study in how much modern investment can still move the needle in Bordeaux.

wines.why_this_wine: Pomerol has no classification and includes some of the most expensive wines on earth (Pétrus, Le Pin), so an affordable, authentic entry point is precious. De Sales is Pomerol's largest estate, making enough wine to actually be attainable, while still showing the plush, clay-driven Merlot character the appellation is famous for.
wines.tasting_notes: Medium ruby-garnet. Ripe plum, red cherry, and a touch of truffle and damp earth typical of Pomerol's iron-rich clay. Soft, plush tannins, moderate acidity, and a warm, generous mid-palate — approachable earlier than most Left Bank wines at a similar price.
wines.winery_info: Château de Sales has belonged to the same family (the de Laage lineage) for centuries and is built around an imposing 17th-century manor house, unusual for tiny Pomerol, where most estates are just a few hectares. At roughly 47 hectares, it is by far the appellation's largest property.
wines.historical_significance: Pomerol was historically overlooked — it was excluded from the 1855 Classification entirely and has refused to adopt one since — yet rose through the 20th century on reputation alone to become one of the most prized (and priciest) appellations in the world, proof that in Bordeaux, the glass can outrank the certificate.

wines.wine_name: Château Beau-Séjour Bécot, Saint-Émilion, 1er Grand Cru Classé B
wines.why_this_wine: A genuine comeback story: this estate was controversially demoted from Premier Grand Cru Classé in 1985 after a boundary dispute, then clawed its way back in 1996 through relentless quality improvements. The 2019 was ranked #11 in Wine Spectator's Top 100 Wines of 2022 — vindication in the glass.
wines.tasting_notes: Deep, glossy garnet. Black cherry, red plum, and violet aromatics with mocha, graphite, and a subtle limestone minerality from the plateau vineyard. Rich but well-balanced, with fine, polished tannins, good acid lift, and a long, refined finish.
wines.winery_info: Owned by brothers Gérard and Julien Bécot, whose family has farmed vines here since the 1960s, the estate occupies a prime south-facing limestone plateau adjoining the town of Saint-Émilion itself, one of the appellation's most coveted sites.
wines.historical_significance: Saint-Émilion's classification is unique in Bordeaux for being periodically revised (roughly every ten years) rather than frozen in time like the 1855 Médoc ranking. Beau-Séjour Bécot's demotion-then-reinstatement is one of the classification's most-cited case studies in how quality investment can be recognized within a single generation.

reviews.note: 2019 vintage ranked #11 in the Wine Spectator Top 100 Wines of 2022.

wines.wine_name: Château Figeac, Saint-Émilion, 1er Grand Cru Classé A
wines.grape_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot (roughly equal thirds)
wines.why_this_wine: Figeac is the great exception that proves the Left/Right Bank rule: its unusually gravelly soil (more typical of the Médoc) lets it plant serious Cabernet, giving a Right Bank wine with genuinely Left Bank structure. Its 2022 promotion to the region's very top tier, alongside a perfect-score 2020, makes this a must-taste for understanding Saint-Émilion's diversity.
wines.tasting_notes: Deep garnet-ruby. An aromatically complex nose of blackcurrant and red cherry alongside cedar, tobacco leaf, and violet — more Pauillac-like than typical plush Saint-Émilion. Firm, fine-grained tannins, vibrant acidity, and remarkable length, built for extended cellaring rather than immediate pleasure.
wines.winery_info: Long stewarded by the Manoncourt family and now overseen by the Cuvelier family (also of Léoville Poyferré) with consulting from renowned oenologist Michel Rolland, Figeac sits on a distinctive gravel bank adjacent to Cheval Blanc and Pomerol, giving it soil more akin to the Médoc than the limestone plateau most of Saint-Émilion sits on.
wines.historical_significance: In the landmark 2022 Saint-Émilion Classification, Figeac was elevated to Premier Grand Cru Classé A — joining only Cheval Blanc, Ausone, Pavie, and Angelus at Bordeaux's Right Bank summit — capping decades in which critics argued the estate had long been underrated relative to its true quality.

wines.wine_name: Château Cheval Blanc, Saint-Émilion, 1er Grand Cru Classé A
wines.why_this_wine: If Mouton Rothschild is the Left Bank's grand statement, Cheval Blanc is the Right Bank's: a wine built on Cabernet Franc rather than Merlot, made from a vineyard literally straddling the Pomerol border, and responsible for one of the most mythologized bottles ever made — the 1947.
wines.tasting_notes: Deep garnet with a hint of purple. A perfumed, floral nose — violets and roses — over black cherry, plum, and a distinctive note of dark chocolate, graphite, and dried herbs. The palate is silky rather than heavy, with fine, velvety tannins, remarkable aromatic persistence, and a seamless, elegant finish.
wines.winery_info: Owned since 1998 by a partnership between LVMH's Bernard Arnault and Belgian industrialist Albert Frère, Cheval Blanc sits on a rare gravel-and-clay mix at the very edge of Saint-Émilion, bordering Pomerol, which explains its atypical Cabernet Franc dominance for the Right Bank.
wines.historical_significance: Cheval Blanc has held Saint-Émilion's top rank since the classification's creation in 1955, and its 1947 vintage — famously thick, port-like, and nearly volatile from the era's extreme heat — is still cited by critics as one of the greatest wines ever produced, a touchstone for what Bordeaux is capable of in a perfect year.

wines.why_this_wine: This is the new-wave 'starter wine' of the Right Bank: a friendly, inexpensive label built by the Pomerol producers behind Château Clinet to introduce drinkers to soft, plush Merlot character without any of the Pomerol price tag — a modern négociant strategy mirroring what Clarendelle does for the Left Bank.
wines.tasting_notes: Bright ruby-red. Juicy red and black plum, cherry, and a touch of vanilla and soft spice from light oak aging. Round, easy-drinking tannins and fresh acidity make it immediately approachable, no cellar required.
wines.winery_info: Produced under the umbrella of the team behind Château Clinet, one of Pomerol's most celebrated modern estates (closely associated with consulting oenologist Michel Rolland's rise to fame in the 1980s-90s), Ronan by Clinet channels that same Merlot expertise into a widely available, easy-drinking label.
wines.historical_significance: The rise of accessible négociant labels attached to famous Pomerol names is itself a 'new wave' phenomenon of the last 20-25 years — a direct market response to skyrocketing grand vin prices, letting everyday drinkers taste a house style that would otherwise be completely out of reach.

wines.classification: Négociant-style label from a 1er Grand Cru Classé A house
wines.why_this_wine: Angelus is Bordeaux's other great modernization story: a Grand Cru Classé that willed its way, through decades of relentless reinvestment, to the very top of Saint-Émilion. N°3 lets you taste that house style — polished, seductive, internationally minded — at a fraction of the grand vin's price.
wines.tasting_notes: Vivid garnet-ruby. Ripe black cherry and blackberry, violet, and a touch of espresso and toasted oak spice. Smooth, well-upholstered tannins and a plush, generous mid-palate, with the polish and immediacy the Angelus style is known for.
wines.winery_info: Angelus is led by the de Boüard de Laforest family, above all Hubert de Boüard, whose decades-long, science-driven campaign — new gravity-flow cellars, radical vineyard reorganization, and famously precise selection — transformed the estate's standing and reputation from the 1980s onward.
wines.historical_significance: Angelus was promoted from Grand Cru Classé to Premier Grand Cru Classé B in 1996, then to the ultra-elite Premier Grand Cru Classé A in the 2012 classification, standing alongside Cheval Blanc and Ausone. It also became globally famous as the château prominently featured in the James Bond films Casino Royale and Spectre — a rare crossover into pop culture for a Bordeaux Grand Cru.

wines.wine_name: Château Valandraud, Saint-Émilion, 1er Grand Cru Classé B
wines.why_this_wine: This is the origin story of the entire 'new wave' in a single bottle. Valandraud is the wine that started the garagiste movement — proof that talent and obsession could beat centuries of classification, and the single most important symbol of how the last 30 years reshaped Bordeaux's power structure.
wines.tasting_notes: Deep, near-opaque purple-garnet. Rich black and blue fruit — blackberry, black cherry, blueberry — layered with mocha, dark chocolate, licorice, and a hint of dried flowers from careful new-oak aging. Lush, velvety, and concentrated, with ripe, well-integrated tannins and a long, opulent, generously fruited finish.
wines.winery_info: Created in 1991 by Jean-Luc Thunevin, a former bank employee with no formal winemaking training, and his wife Murielle Andraud (the name 'Valandraud' fuses 'Val' and 'Andraud'), the wine was first made from under a hectare of vines, hand-sorted and vinified in a literal garage behind their house in Saint-Émilion.
wines.historical_significance: Denied any appellation status for years by an establishment that considered it an upstart, Valandraud instead built a cult following through sheer quality and bold pricing — igniting the 1990s 'garage wine' phenomenon across the Right Bank. Vindication came in stages: Saint-Émilion Grand Cru Classé status in 2006, and Premier Grand Cru Classé B in 2012, formally admitting the outsider to Bordeaux's most rarefied tier.

wines.why_this_wine: No introduction to Bordeaux is complete without its dry whites, and Carbonnieux is one of the oldest, most historic names making them. It shows how Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, blended and given real structure from gravel-terroir fruit, can age and evolve in a way most New World Sauvignon Blanc never does.
wines.tasting_notes: Pale gold with green highlights. Citrus zest, white peach, and honeysuckle aromas over a distinct flinty, mineral core. Crisp, vibrant acidity balanced by a touch of textural richness from partial barrel aging, finishing clean, long, and saline.
wines.winery_info: One of the most ancient wine estates in all of Bordeaux, Carbonnieux was cultivated by Benedictine monks from the Priory of Sainte-Croix from the Middle Ages onward, giving it a documented winemaking history that predates the 1855 Classification by centuries.
wines.historical_significance: A well-loved (if not fully verified) legend holds that Carbonnieux's white wine was shipped to the Ottoman Sultan labeled as 'mineral water,' since Islamic law forbade alcohol — a story that, true or not, speaks to just how long this property has been prized far beyond Bordeaux's borders.

wines.why_this_wine: Sauternes is Bordeaux's third pillar, and no new wine lover should skip it. Guiraud is one of the region's great classified estates and a pioneer of organic viticulture among the Sauternais's classified growths — proof the region's oldest sweet-wine tradition can also lead on modern farming.
wines.tasting_notes: Bright gold. Honeyed apricot, candied orange peel, and saffron on the nose, with a lush, unctuous palate of dried fruit, vanilla, and toasted nuts. Crucially, vibrant acidity keeps the intense sweetness balanced rather than cloying, with a very long, honeyed finish.
wines.winery_info: A Premier Cru Classé in the 1855 Sauternes ranking, Guiraud has been owned since 2006 by a consortium that included the Peugeot family (of the automobile dynasty) among other investors, who pushed the estate to become fully organic-certified by 2011 — a first among the classified Sauternes châteaux.
wines.historical_significance: Sauternes and Barsac were the only sweet wines included in the 1855 Classification alongside the Médoc reds, a testament to how highly noble-rot wines were once prized; Château d'Yquem was the sole wine awarded the unique rank of Premier Cru Supérieur. Guiraud, one of the era's original Premiers Crus, has spent the last two decades proving that quality here can be paired with genuinely sustainable farming.
